note: Hand-written reviewed protocols (the maker's own list). merge.py checks every link opens and that nothing comes from a bench-protocol source, then writes them into src/mygeeky/data/curated.json. myGeeKy teaches analysis, never laboratory work: see src/mygeeky/safety.py.

protocols.title: Git and GitHub for working with others
protocols.summary: Branches, pull requests and reviews: how a team works on one repo without stepping on each other. For anyone whose code has started to matter to someone else.

stages.title: Git on your own machine
can: I can commit, look at the history and undo a change I regret
I know what the staging area is for
I can get myself out of a mess without deleting the folder

items.title: Pro Git
items.note: The whole of Git, free, and the only reference you'll keep coming back to. Chapters 2 and 3 are enough to start.

items.title: Learn Git Branching
items.note: Branches drawn as you type the commands. Half an hour here saves weeks of confusion.

items.title: The Missing Semester of Your CS Education
items.note: MIT's lecture on version control: what Git actually stores, which makes the commands make sense.

stages.title: Branches, and fixing history
can: I can rebase or merge a branch and explain which I'd choose
I can resolve a conflict without panicking
I know what not to force-push, and why

items.title: Oh My Git!
items.note: A card game that teaches branching, rebasing and conflicts. Free, and more fun than it has any right to be.

items.title: GitHub flow
items.note: The short branching rule most teams actually follow, in one page.

items.title: Dangit, Git!?!
items.note: The fix for whatever you just did, in plain words. Keep it open.

stages.title: Pull requests and reviews
can: I can open a pull request that a reviewer can actually read
I can review someone's code and leave a useful comment
I can keep a branch up to date while it's being reviewed

items.title: GitHub Skills
items.note: Short hands-on courses from GitHub itself: pull requests, reviews and Actions, each done inside a real repo.

items.title: Google's code review guide
items.note: What a reviewer looks for, and how to be one. Short, and the standard most teams borrow from.

items.title: Conventional Commits
items.note: A commit-message rule a whole team can follow, which later gives you a changelog for free.

stages.title: One repo, as a team
can: Our repo has a branch rule and a check that runs on every pull request

items.title: GitHub Actions: your first workflow
items.note: The check that runs on every pull request, in about ten lines.

items.title: First Contributions
items.note: A repo whose whole purpose is to accept your practice pull request. Do it once with no stakes.

stages.title: Use it in your own work

protocols.title: Algorithms and data structures, for interviews and for real work
protocols.summary: The handful of patterns most interview questions come from, and the thinking behind them, without grinding puzzles for six months.

stages.title: The structures themselves
can: I can say when I'd use a hash map instead of a list, and why
I can read O(n log n) and say what it means for 10 million items
I can write a loop over a tree without looking it up

items.title: Open Data Structures
items.note: Free, short, and in the language you choose. Each structure with the cost of every operation.

items.title: MIT 6.006: Introduction to Algorithms
items.note: The lectures, notes and problem sets, free. The honest version of this subject.

items.title: TheAlgorithms/Python
items.note: Every classic algorithm, implemented plainly, to read rather than to copy.

stages.title: The patterns behind the questions
can: I can spot a two-pointer, sliding-window or BFS problem from its wording
I can write a recursion and say what its base case is
I can get from a working answer to a faster one on purpose

items.title: Competitive Programmer's Handbook
items.note: Free. The patterns, in order, with the maths kept to what you need.

items.title: NeetCode: the roadmap
items.note: The problems grouped by pattern, in an order that builds. Use the grouping even if you practise elsewhere.

items.title: CSES Problem Set
items.note: A graded set that matches the handbook, with no gimmicks.

stages.title: The interview itself
can: I can talk through my thinking while I write, not after
I ask about the input before I start
I can test my own answer on the awkward cases

items.title: Tech Interview Handbook
items.note: What happens in the room, how to practise for it, and what to say. Free and plainly written.

items.title: System Design Primer
items.note: For the design round, which most people meet unprepared.

stages.title: Build one thing with them
can: I've written something non-trivial where the data structure choice mattered

items.title: Build Your Own X
items.note: Write your own database, git, or regex engine, following someone who did. Where the structures stop being abstract.

stages.title: Use it in your own work

protocols.title: Your first web app, start to finish
protocols.summary: One small app with a database behind it, put online where other people can use it. The shape every later project reuses.

stages.title: How the web actually works
can: I can say what happens between a click and a page appearing
I know what a GET and a POST are for
I can read a 404 or a 500 and know whose problem it is

items.title: MDN: learn web development
items.note: The reference the whole industry uses, free. Start with the server-side part.

items.title: FastAPI tutorial
items.note: A working API in a few lines of Python, each line explained. The gentlest start if you already know Python.

items.title: Flask tutorial
items.note: A small blog app, built step by step, with the database and logins included.

stages.title: A database behind it
can: I can design two or three tables that don't repeat themselves
I can write the queries my app needs without an ORM
I know what an index is for

items.title: Select Star SQL
items.note: SQL you write in the page, on real data. Free, and quietly excellent.

items.title: Django's own tutorial
items.note: The heavier framework, which hands you an admin page and a login system. Worth seeing once.

items.title: Use the index, Luke
items.note: Why your query is slow. The one thing most self-taught developers never read.

stages.title: Put it online
can: Someone else can open my app at a URL
My secrets are not in the repo
I can see what went wrong when it breaks at 2am

items.title: Full Stack open
items.note: The University of Helsinki's free course, front to back, with deployment. Long, and worth it.

items.title: The Twelve-Factor App
items.note: Twelve short rules that keep an app deployable. Read it before you need it.

items.title: OWASP Top Ten
items.note: The ten ways apps get broken into. Know them before you put a login on anything.

stages.title: One real app, finished
can: I've finished and deployed one small app that someone else uses

items.title: RealWorld example apps
items.note: The same app written in dozens of stacks. Read the one near yours to see what 'done' looks like.

stages.title: Use it in your own work

protocols.title: Machine learning that works outside a notebook
protocols.summary: Getting from a tutorial model to one that holds up: honest validation, the leakage that quietly ruins results, and putting it somewhere it can be used.

stages.title: The basics, properly
can: I can split data into train and test and say why
I can tell classification from regression and pick a fitting measure
I can fit and score a model with scikit-learn on my own

items.title: scikit-learn MOOC (Inria)
items.note: Free, with notebooks and exercises, by the people who write scikit-learn.

items.title: An Introduction to Statistical Learning
items.note: The free book that explains what the methods are doing, in R and in Python.

items.title: Practical Deep Learning for Coders
items.note: fast.ai's course: working results from the first lesson, theory when you need it.

stages.title: Validation you can defend
can: I can set up cross-validation that respects groups and time
I can name three ways data leaks between train and test
I know why my test score will look worse in the real world

items.title: Leakage and the reproducibility crisis in ML-based science
items.note: Kapoor & Narayanan: eight kinds of leakage, and the published results they broke. The most useful afternoon in this protocol.

items.title: Rules of Machine Learning
items.note: Google's 43 rules, in order of when you'll need them. Rule 1 is 'don't be afraid to launch without machine learning'.

items.title: Model Cards for Model Reporting
items.note: What to write down about a model so someone else can judge it.

stages.title: Out of the notebook
can: My training runs from a script, not from cells I ran in some order
I can say which data and which code made a given model
Someone else can get a prediction out of it without me

items.title: Made With ML
items.note: Free, and the only popular course that treats testing, packaging and serving as part of the job.

items.title: Machine Learning Operations (ml-ops.org)
items.note: The vocabulary and the moving parts, without a vendor attached.

items.title: awesome-production-machine-learning
items.note: The tools, grouped by what they're for, when you need to pick one.

stages.title: One model, used by someone
can: I've taken one model from data to something a person can actually use

items.title: Papers with Code
items.note: A published result with its code, to reproduce before you trust it. The best honesty exercise there is.

stages.title: Use it in your own work

protocols.title: Your first pull request to someone else's project
protocols.summary: Finding an issue worth taking, reading a codebase you didn't write, and getting a change merged without annoying anyone.

stages.title: How a project works
can: I can find a project's CONTRIBUTING file and follow it
I know what a maintainer's time is worth, and what to ask for
I can fork, branch and open a pull request without help

items.title: Open Source Guides
items.note: GitHub's own guide to a first contribution, and the one most maintainers wish people had read.

items.title: First Contributions
items.note: A repo built to accept your practice pull request. Get the mechanics wrong here, where it doesn't matter.

items.title: How to Contribute to Open Source (freeCodeCamp)
items.note: The same ground again in plainer words, if the guides feel abstract.

stages.title: Reading code you didn't write
can: I can get a strange project running on my machine
I can find where a bug lives using the tests
I can make the smallest change that fixes it

items.title: The Architecture of Open Source Applications
items.note: Real projects explained by the people who built them. Free.

items.title: Google's code review guide: the reviewer
items.note: What reviewers look at, which is what your pull request should answer in advance.

stages.title: Find a real issue
can: I've found an issue I understand in a project I use
I asked whether it's still wanted before writing code
My pull request says what it changes and why, in two lines

items.title: Good First Issue
items.note: Issues maintainers have marked as a good place to start, across many projects.

items.title: CodeTriage
items.note: Sends you one open issue a day from a project you choose. Low effort, and it builds the habit.

items.title: Up For Grabs
items.note: The same idea, a different list. Between the three you'll find something in your language.

stages.title: Merged
can: Something I wrote is in a project I don't own

items.title: myGeeKy's own ideas repo
items.note: If you'd rather start somewhere small: this is where myGeeKy's own issues and protocols live.

protocols.title: Images into numbers, with Fiji
protocols.summary: Measuring the images on your disk without fooling yourself: what a pixel value is, which measurement answers your question, and a script that measures a whole folder the same way.

stages.title: Fiji, and what an image is
can: I can open, scale and measure an image in Fiji
I know what bit depth and a lookup table are
I can set the scale from the file's own metadata, not by guessing

items.title: Fiji (ImageJ)
items.note: The free software, with the plugins already in. Everything here assumes it.

items.title: ImageJ: the basics of image processing
items.note: What a digital image is, from the project itself. Short, and it prevents most later mistakes.

items.title: ImageJ user guide
items.note: The reference for every menu item, free.

stages.title: Measurements you can defend
can: I know what saturated pixels do to a measurement, and how to spot them in the histogram
I can say which measurement (intensity, area, count, ratio) answers my question
I record every adjustment I make, and never one that changes the data

items.title: Avoiding twisted pixels: ethical guidelines for digital images
items.note: What you may and may not do to an image, with examples of what crosses the line.

items.title: A guide to accurate reporting in digital image processing
items.note: What to write down about how an image was processed, from the Journal of Cell Science.

items.title: ImageJ: image intensity processing
items.note: Histograms, look-up tables and what 'brightness' really means to a measurement.

stages.title: Counting and measuring, repeatably
can: I can threshold and count objects, and name the method I used
I can write a macro so every image in a folder gets the same treatment
I can measure colocalisation without reading more into it than it says

items.title: ImageJ: segmentation
items.note: The thresholding and segmentation methods, and when each one fits.

items.title: ImageJ macro language
items.note: Record what you clicked, then run it on a folder. The step that turns clicking into a method.

items.title: CellProfiler
items.note: Free pipelines for measuring thousands of objects, when macros stop being enough.

stages.title: From measurements to a result
can: My unit of analysis is what I actually compared, not every object I measured
I plot every object and every replicate, not a mean alone
My numbers come out of a script, so they can be remade

items.title: Nested analyses of cell-based data
items.note: SuperPlots: how to plot and test measurements without pretending each object is independent.

items.title: Fundamentals of Data Visualization
items.note: Free, and the fastest way to stop making misleading figures.

stages.title: Reproduce a published measurement
can: I've reproduced a published image measurement from its own description

items.title: Papers with Code
items.note: Published image-analysis work with its code, to rerun before you trust it.

stages.title: Use it in your own work

protocols.goal: your first analysis of your own data
protocols.title: From Excel to R, with your own data
protocols.summary: Your own spreadsheet, read into R, cleaned, plotted and tested. Written for people who have never programmed, and who have real data waiting.

stages.title: R, with no programming before
can: I can install R and RStudio and find my way around the windows
I can read my own Excel file into R
I can look at the first rows and say what each column is

items.title: Hands-On Programming with R
items.note: Free, and written for people with no programming at all. Three small projects, nothing assumed.

items.title: R for Reproducible Scientific Analysis (Software Carpentry)
items.note: The lesson taught in workshops worldwide, free to work through alone.

items.title: readxl
items.note: Reading .xlsx straight into R, including the sheet and the range. One line, and your data is in.

stages.title: A tidy table, not a tidy-looking one
can: I can turn a wide sheet with merged headers into one row per measurement
I can keep my raw file untouched and do the cleaning in the script
I can spot the typos and units problems my spreadsheet was hiding

items.title: R for Data Science (2e)
items.note: The free standard. Chapters on data import, tidying and transforming are exactly this step.

items.title: Tidy Data
items.note: The short paper that explains what shape a table should be in, and why it makes everything after easier.

items.title: Data organization in spreadsheets
items.note: Broman & Woo: how to keep the spreadsheet itself sane, before R ever sees it. Change one habit from this.

stages.title: Your first plot and test
can: I can plot my own measurements with every replicate showing
I can run the test that suits my design and read the output
I can save a figure at a size and resolution a journal accepts

items.title: Data Analysis and Visualisation in R for Ecologists (Data Carpentry)
items.note: Real messy data, plotted and summarised. Nothing to do with ecology, really.

items.title: ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis
items.note: Free. How the plotting grammar fits together, so you stop copying examples.

items.title: Learning Statistics with R
items.note: Free, long, and kind: statistics and R taught together, assuming neither.

stages.title: One analysis, from file to figure
can: One script takes my raw file and makes the figure, with nothing done by hand

items.title: Quarto: get started
items.note: Put the text, the code and the figures in one document that rebuilds itself. This is what makes it reproducible.

items.title: TidyTuesday
items.note: A new dataset every week, and hundreds of people's scripts for it. The best way to see how others do it.

stages.title: Use it in your own work

protocols.goal: choosing and running the right test
protocols.title: Statistics for experiments: which test, and why
protocols.summary: t-test, ANOVA and their assumptions, in the words of an experiment: replicates, controls, and what a p-value does and does not tell you.

stages.title: What your numbers are
can: I can say what my unit of analysis is for a given experiment
I know the difference between a technical and a biological replicate
I can describe my data before testing it: mean, spread, and a plot

items.title: Points of Significance (Nature Methods)
items.note: Two-page columns, free, each on one idea: error bars, replication, significance. Start here and read them in order.

items.title: Introduction to Modern Statistics
items.note: Free, clear, and full of real data. The textbook if you want one.

items.title: StatQuest
items.note: Short videos that explain one test at a time, drawn out slowly. Many bench scientists learn this way.

stages.title: Choosing the test
can: I can pick between a t-test, a paired t-test and ANOVA for my design
I can state the assumptions of the test I chose
I know what to do about multiple comparisons

items.title: Handbook of Biological Statistics
items.note: McDonald's free handbook: for each test, when to use it, how, and what to report. The most practical thing on this list.

items.title: The ASA statement on p-values
items.note: Six short principles from the American Statistical Association. Two pages that change how you write results.

items.title: Scientists rise up against statistical significance
items.note: Why 'not significant' doesn't mean 'no effect'. Free, and short.

stages.title: Running it, and reporting it
can: I can run my test in R or GraphPad and read every number it gives back
I report effect size and uncertainty, not only a p-value
I can work out a sample size before the experiment, not after

items.title: Learning Statistics with R
items.note: Free. Does the test in R next to the explanation, which is the fastest way to trust the output.

items.title: G*Power
items.note: Free software for sample size and power. Use it before you start, even roughly.

items.title: Beyond bar and line graphs
items.note: Plot the data, not a summary of it. The figure change that makes the statistics honest.

stages.title: Reanalyse one of your own experiments
can: I've redone the statistics of one finished experiment, and can defend every choice

items.title: Nested analyses of cell-based data (SuperPlots)
items.note: A worked example of the mistake almost everyone makes with replicates, and how to fix the plot and the test together.

stages.title: Use it in your own work

protocols.title: Figures your reviewers won't ask you to redo
protocols.summary: One script that makes the figure, so it can be remade when the data changes: axes, colour, honesty, and the file the journal actually wants.

stages.title: What makes a figure readable
can: I can choose the plot type that suits my data, not the one I always use
I can label axes with units so no caption is needed to read them
I can tell when my figure is hiding the data

items.title: Fundamentals of Data Visualization
items.note: Free. Each chapter shows a bad figure and the better one, with the reason.

items.title: Ten Simple Rules for Better Figures
items.note: Ten rules, two pages, open access. The fastest improvement available to anyone.

items.title: Points of View (Nature Methods)
items.note: The visualisation companion to Points of Significance: colour, salience and layout, one page each.

stages.title: Colour, and who can read it
can: I use a palette that survives colour blindness and a black-and-white printer
I never use a rainbow scale for continuous data, and can say why
My colours mean the same thing in every panel

items.title: ColorBrewer
items.note: Palettes chosen for maps and plots, with colour-blind and print-safe filters.

items.title: The misuse of colour in science communication
items.note: Why jet and rainbow scales mislead, with the alternatives. Open access.

items.title: viridis
items.note: The default good answer for continuous colour, in R and Python alike.

stages.title: The figure, from a script
can: My figure is made by a script I can rerun when the data changes
I can build a multi-panel figure with consistent sizes and fonts
I can export at the width, font size and format the journal asks for

items.title: ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis
items.note: Free. The R side, including arranging panels and saving at an exact size.

items.title: Matplotlib tutorials
items.note: The Python side, from the project itself.

items.title: The R Graph Gallery
items.note: Hundreds of plots with their code. Find the one you want and take the code.

stages.title: Remake one of your own figures
can: One of my published or submitted figures now comes out of a script, identical

items.note: Text, code and figures in one document that rebuilds itself. Then a data fix never means redrawing by hand.
